key_facts: US regulators (FCC) approved SpaceX's plan to launch up to a million satellites into orbit to build orbital data centres, described as the first approval of its kind.
The project, known as Starmind, would use solar power in orbit to process AI data and send results back to Earth; FCC said it will "support America's booming super intelligence economy".

Under the licence, deployment must begin no later than November 2033, with 10% deployed by November 2035 and 50% by November 2038; SpaceX plans to launch its first Starmind satellite next year. It is unclear whether a million satellites will actually be launched.

Experts cited by the BBC say launching and protecting orbital hardware remains expensive, with space debris and collision risk among the concerns; Google and Blue Origin are also exploring orbital data centres.
importance_reason: Regulatory approval of a speculative, long-horizon infrastructure project with no direct near-term market impact; mainly a sector/tech story.
market_link: Possible long-term demand signal for space and satellite infrastructure and AI compute, but the effect on listed markets is not clear from the source.

region: Germany / EU (dispute involves US company Fender and German retailer Thomann)
key_facts: Fender Stratocaster body shape, designed in the US in the early 1950s and not trademarked when first made, is subject to a copyright dispute: a Düsseldorf court in December 2025 granted Fender copyright protection for the design in Germany in a default judgment, as the Chinese defendant Yiwu Philharmonic did not appear.

In March 2026 Fender sent cease-and-desist letters to dozens of retailers and manufacturers demanding they stop making and selling Strat-style guitars for Germany and other EU countries, regardless of where produced. In June, Thomann filed an 'action of non-infringement'; in July, Fender sued Thomann in a German court for copyright infringement.
Thomann sold over 112,000 Strat-style guitars in 2025, including more than 16,000 made by Fender and its subsidiary Squier.
importance_reason: Feature-style story about an IP dispute in the musical instruments retail sector with no direct market, macro or price impact.

key_facts: The UK government and the EU are set to publish texts of two treaties on Thursday afternoon, agreed last week as part of a new UK-EU deal, along with UK legislation (the Cutting Costs Bill) to enact the bulk of the deal.

The treaties reportedly contain a 10-year termination clause: if one party ends the agreement within that period, it would have to pay to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which has been significantly scaled back under the new deal. Badenoch and Farage have suggested they would refuse to pay.

The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost to agricultural exports; the BBC notes the cost reduction may not be visible to consumers at the checkout.

The treaties will affect UK aviation and maritime industries through alignment with EU emissions schemes; the legislation includes secondary legislation powers (so-called 'Henry VIII powers') for ministers to align UK and EU laws.
importance_reason: Significant UK-EU trade and regulatory development with sectoral effects, but no direct rate decision or market-moving price shock.
market_link: Potential effects on UK food exporters, aviation and maritime sectors via reduced border costs and alignment with EU emissions trading; the 16% agri-export forecast is an internal estimate cited by the BBC, not a confirmed outcome.
